cards.front: A GTPase is on when it holds {{c1::GTP}} and off when it holds GDP, which is GTP minus its third phosphate.
cards.quote: A GTPase cuts the GTP it binds: on with GTP, off with GDP, which is GTP minus its third phosphate.

cards.front: A guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) promotes release of bound {{c1::GDP}} so that GTP can load.
cards.quote: A guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) promotes release of bound GDP.

cards.front: Once a GEF has released GDP from a GTPase, why does the empty site usually fill with GTP?
cards.back: GTP is far more plentiful than GDP in the cell, so GTP usually takes the empty place.
cards.quote: GTP is far more plentiful than GDP in the cell, so GTP usually takes the empty place.

cards.front: For a heterotrimeric G protein under a receptor, which protein is the GEF?
cards.back: The occupied receptor itself.
cards.quote: For a heterotrimeric G protein under a receptor, the occupied receptor is the GEF.

cards.front: Intrinsic GTP cutting is slow; a {{c1::GTPase-activating protein (GAP)}} binds the GTPase and accelerates it.
cards.quote: Intrinsic cutting is slow; a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) binds the GTPase and accelerates it.

cards.front: Why can one occupied receptor drive a large response even though each G protein reloads slowly by itself?
cards.back: One occupied receptor loads many freely moving G proteins in succession, and each loaded G protein can switch on a cyclase of its own.
cards.quote: one occupied receptor can load many freely moving G proteins in succession

cards.front: For first-order GTP cutting, mean time on = {{c1::1 / k(cut)}}.
cards.quote: mean time on = 1 / k(cut)

cards.front: In the equation for mean time on, why do the hormone and receptor not appear?
cards.back: They start the clock, but the equation describes one already-loaded switch, whose time on depends only on how fast it cuts GTP.
cards.quote: The hormone and the receptor start the clock, but they do not appear in the equation; it describes one loaded switch.

cards.front: A purified G alpha cuts GTP with k(cut) = 0.02 per second. Saturating RGS raises it to 1.0 per second. Give the two mean lifetimes and the factor by which the lifetime changes.
cards.back: 1/0.02 = 50 s and 1/1.0 = 1 s, so the lifetime is 50-fold shorter.
cards.why: A rate constant is not a duration; take its reciprocal.
cards.quote: The means are 1/0.02 = 50 seconds and 1/1.0 = 1 second, a 50-fold shorter lifetime.

cards.front: A loaded GTPase stays on for a mean of 8 seconds with first-order cutting. What is k(cut), and what is the mean time on if a GAP raises k(cut) 10-fold?
cards.back: k(cut) = 1/8 = 0.125 per second. At 10 times that rate the mean time on is 1/1.25 = 0.8 s.
cards.quote: mean time on = 1 / k(cut)

cards.front: After a hormone is washed out, what determines how long each already-loaded G protein keeps signaling?
cards.back: Its own GTP-cutting clock. Loading nearly stops after washout, and each loaded protein runs out its own time on.
cards.quote: after washout, loading nearly stops and each loaded protein runs out its own clock.

cards.front: Cyclic AMP falls slowly after hormone washout. What extra measurement separates slow GTP cutting from slow cyclic AMP clearance, and how is it read?
cards.back: Measure GTP-bound Gs alpha too. If it returns to GDP quickly while cyclic AMP stays high, downstream clearance is slow. If GTP-bound Gs alpha persists, the delay lies at or before its off step.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that the off step of the GTPase sets its time on.
cards.quote: If GTP-bound Gs alpha persists, the delay lies at or before its off step.

cards.front: What does each of Gs, Gi and Gq act on?
cards.back: Gs switches adenylyl cyclase on, Gi turns it down, and Gq switches on phospholipase C-beta.
cards.quote: Gs switches adenylyl cyclase on, Gi turns it down, and Gq switches on phospholipase C-beta.

cards.front: Which trimeric G protein families have RGS proteins as major GAPs, and which family does not?
cards.back: Gi- and Gq-family subunits do; Gs does not.
cards.quote: For Gi- and Gq-family subunits, but not Gs, major GAPs include RGS proteins, regulators of G-protein signaling.

cards.front: How do RGS4 and GAIP change a Gi-family G protein, and why can more of them shorten a Gi-coupled response?
cards.back: They make it cut GTP at least 40 times faster in vitro. GAIP binds the GTP-holding form, so it acts only while the switch is on.
cards.quote: RGS4 and its relative GAIP make a Gi-family G protein cut at least 40 times faster in vitro.

cards.front: Gq activates phospholipase C-beta, which then speeds Gq's GTP cutting. Is this connection reinforcing or self-limiting?
cards.back: Self-limiting. The effector that active Gq turns on accelerates Gq's return to GDP, so output and shutoff are coupled.
cards.quote: The effector that active Gq turns on accelerates Gq's return to GDP, so the same encounter couples output to shutoff.

cards.front: For Ras, which protein is the GEF, and which proteins are its GAPs?
cards.back: SOS is the GEF. Neurofibromin and p120 GAP are the GAPs.
cards.quote: SOS, short for son of sevenless, is its exchange factor, and growth-factor receptors recruit it to the membrane.

cards.front: In vitro, a crude extract sped normal Ras's GTP cutting more than 200-fold but did nothing to the oncogenic mutant. What does this show about the mutant?
cards.back: The oncogenic mutant does not respond to the GAP activity, so its off step stays slow.
cards.quote: a factor that sped normal Ras's GTP cutting more than 200-fold in vitro and did nothing to the oncogenic mutant

cards.front: What did the Ras structure holding an uncuttable GTP analogue show about its fold, and what does that imply?
cards.back: The fold matches EF-Tu, a bacterial protein that delivers tRNAs to the ribosome. Ras and EF-Tu inherited the same ancient fold from a common ancestor.
cards.quote: Ras and EF-Tu inherited the same ancient fold from a common ancestor.

cards.front: What do the Rho and Rab small-GTPase families each regulate?
cards.back: Rho: the actin cytoskeleton and cell shape. Rab: vesicle traffic between membranes.
cards.quote: Rho: the actin cytoskeleton and cell shape.

cards.front: Why can a G protein bind Gpp(NH)p but not cut it?
cards.back: In Gpp(NH)p the oxygen bridging the last two phosphates is replaced by NH, so the G protein can bind it and cannot cut it.
cards.quote: In Gpp(NH)p the oxygen bridging the last two phosphates is replaced by NH, so the G protein can bind it and cannot cut it.

cards.front: Frog red blood cell membranes were treated with isoproterenol plus Gpp(NH)p. After washing, adenylyl cyclase stayed on and propranolol could not reverse it. What does this show?
cards.back: The persistent state lies downstream of the receptor, in the G protein holding the uncuttable nucleotide. A receptor locked on would still be turned off by the blocker.
cards.quote: It did not, which places the persistent state downstream of the receptor, in the G protein holding the uncuttable nucleotide.

cards.front: What does cholera toxin do to Gs, and what is the result for cyclic AMP?
cards.back: The toxin is an enzyme that splits NAD and can attach its ADP-ribose group to arginine. Its target is Gs, and the attached group blocks the step that switches Gs off, so cyclic AMP stays high.
cards.quote: It splits NAD and can attach its ADP-ribose group to the amino acid arginine.

cards.front: Trace how persistent Gs activation in an intestinal cell leads to watery diarrhea in cholera.
cards.back: With cyclic AMP high, the intestinal cell opens CFTR chloride channels. Salt leaves into the gut, water follows, and the result is watery diarrhea.
cards.quote: An intestinal cell responds by opening CFTR chloride channels; salt leaves into the gut, water follows, and the result is the watery diarrhea of cholera.

cards.front: Cells are treated with cholera toxin, then given extra RGS protein. Predict the effect on Gs signal duration.
cards.back: Little or no shortening. The toxin blocks the step that switches Gs off, and RGS proteins do not act on Gs.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: the modified Gs cannot be switched off, and RGS proteins are not GAPs for Gs.
cards.quote: The attached group blocks the step that switches Gs off, so cyclic AMP stays high.

cards.front: Why does Ras G12V stay GTP-bound even when a GAP binds it?
cards.back: Valine puts a bulkier side chain where the GAP's arginine must reach, disrupting the catalytic arrangement. GAP binds without giving its normal acceleration.
cards.quote: Replacing it with valine puts a bulkier side chain where the GAP's arginine must reach and disrupts the catalytic arrangement, so GAP can bind without giving its normal acceleration.

cards.front: How does the defect in Ras Q61 mutants differ from that in G12V?
cards.back: Q61 mutants cut GTP poorly with or without GAP. In G12V, GAP can bind but does not give its normal acceleration.
cards.quote: Q61 mutants cut poorly with or without GAP.

cards.front: A cell expresses Ras Q61K. Extra p120 GAP is added. Does Ras time on shorten much?
cards.back: No. Glutamine 61 helps stabilize the cutting transition state, and Q61 mutants cut poorly with or without GAP, so Ras stays GTP-bound.
cards.quote: Glutamine 61, changed to lysine in the tumor mutant Q61K, helps stabilize the cutting reaction's transition state.

cards.front: Why is Ras S17N rarely GTP-loaded, and what happens even if it holds GTP?
cards.back: Asparagine in place of serine 17 lowers affinity for GTP much more than for GDP. Even holding GTP, it fails to switch on its targets.
cards.quote: Asparagine in place of serine 17 lowers Ras's affinity for GTP much more than for GDP.

cards.front: What is a dominant-negative mutant, in the case of Ras S17N?
cards.back: A mutant that blocks its normal partner. S17N is thought to hold on to exchange factors such as SOS, soaking up what normal Ras needs.
cards.quote: A mutant that blocks its normal partner this way is called dominant-negative.

cards.front: What rescue experiment would support the proposal that Ras S17N suppresses normal Ras by soaking up SOS, and what result would support it?
cards.back: Supply more SOS and measure GTP loading of normal Ras. If loading recovers, the exchange factor was the limiting part S17N had taken up.
cards.quote: Supply more SOS and measure GTP loading of normal Ras.

cards.front: After a growth factor is washed out, GTP-bound Ras is wild type 30% to 4%, G12V 85% to 83%, S17N 2% to 2%. Which step is broken in each mutant?
cards.back: G12V holds GTP after the stimulus ends, so its off step is broken. S17N stays nearly empty of GTP, so its on step is broken.
cards.quote: So Ras is rarely loaded with GTP, and even holding GTP it fails to switch on its targets.

cards.front: Glucagon came off liver membranes with ATP because of contaminating GTP. Why does this show GTP acts as a regulator and not as fuel?
cards.back: The cyclase runs on ATP, and a trace of GTP was enough, so GTP was not used up once per cyclic AMP made.
cards.quote: GTP was not the fuel, because the cyclase runs on ATP, and a trace was enough
cards.section: How the GTP requirement and the transducer were found

cards.front: cyc- lymphoma cells lack the link between receptor and enzyme. A soluble extract from normal cells restored hormone response even with its own cyclase inactivated. What does this show?
cards.back: The transducer is a separate, movable protein that can be supplied from outside the membrane.
cards.quote: The transducer was therefore a separate, movable protein.
cards.section: How the GTP requirement and the transducer were found

cards.front: Extra RGS protein is expressed in a cell with a Gi-coupled receptor. Predict the effect on how often G proteins are loaded and on how long each stays on.
cards.back: Loading frequency is unchanged, since the receptor is the GEF. Each loaded Gi-family protein stays on for a shorter time, so the response shortens.
cards.why: Rests on the split between how often switches are loaded and how long each stays on.
cards.quote: so more of these RGS proteins can shorten a Gi-coupled response.

cards.front: A Ras mutant stays GTP-bound. What measurements would show whether its on step or its off step is changed?
cards.back: Measure GTP loading and GTP cutting separately, with and without GAP. A broken off step cuts poorly even with GAP; a changed on step shows little GTP loading.
cards.why: Rests on the cycle: GEF loads, cutting with GAP shuts off.
cards.quote: Either way Ras stays GTP-bound and keeps signaling.
